# Introduction

TODO(JV): Introduction not drafted. Points the Methods and Results are written to connect
to: raised bogs as ombrotrophic landforms with a climatically bounded distribution
[@joostenMiresPeatlandsEurope2017; @gallego-salaBioclimaticEnvelopeModel2010;
@parviainenClimateEnvelopesMire2007]; the "typical raised bog" region of Europe and its
Norwegian outpost [@tannebergerMiresEuropeRegional2021]; the complete Norwegian inventory
from aerial-photo interpretation [@lyngstadFlybildetolkingAvHogmyr2012;
@lyngstadKartleggingAvTypisk2015]; the management question (restoration prioritisation,
@miljodirektoratetPlanRestaureringAv2020); and the modelling problem that a Norwegian-only
model cannot see the warm edge of the niche because Norway does not contain it.

# Materials and methods

## Study system and question

Typical raised bogs are domed, ombrotrophic peat landforms whose surface is fed only by
precipitation. Their distribution in Europe is confined to a band of climate that is cool
enough to limit evaporation and decomposition but productive enough for *Sphagnum* peat
to accumulate; on the cold and wet side they give way to fens, aapa mires and blanket bogs,
and on the warm and dry side to forest, heath and farmland
[@joostenMiresPeatlandsEurope2017; @tannebergerMiresEuropeRegional2021]. Norway holds the
north-western edge of the typical raised bog region, and Norway's raised bogs therefore sit
at the cool end of the climatic band that supports the landform.

We asked which of Norway's mapped typical raised bogs will still have a climate that
supports a raised bog at the end of this century, and where in Norway such a climate will
exist. Two features of the question shape the analysis. First, the future climate of
Norway's raised bogs lies outside the range of climate that Norway's raised bogs occupy
today, so any model trained on Norwegian data alone is asked to extrapolate. We therefore
recruited data from the rest of the typical raised bog region, where raised bogs and their
warm-side neighbours already occur under the climates Norway is moving into. Second, the
loss of a raised bog under warming does not lead to a single alternative state: the site
may remain peatland of another kind, or it may cease to be peatland at all. We therefore
modelled a three-class response rather than presence and absence, so that the two
ecologically opposite non-bog outcomes are kept apart.

The analysis is organised in four parts: assembling the occurrence data and their labels
(this section and the next three), a model-free description of where the future climate of
today's bogs sits relative to what is observed today, one pooled three-class model and its
projection over Norway, and a cross-validation designed to say how the model behaves when
it is pushed into warmer climates than the bogs it learned from.

## Raised-bog occurrence data

### Norway: a complete aerial-photo inventory

Norwegian raised bogs come from a systematic inventory of typical raised bogs carried out
by stereo interpretation of digital aerial photographs at the NTNU University Museum
between 2012 and 2023 [@lyngstadFlybildetolkingAvHogmyr2012;
@lyngstadKartleggingAvTypisk2015; @lyngstadKartleggingAvTypisk2016;
@lyngstadKartleggingAvTypisk2017; @lyngstadKartleggingAvTypisk2021]. Raised bogs are
domed, with easily visible surface patterns, which makes them well suited to
identification from stereo imagery. Every mire massif in the surveyed areas was assessed,
and massifs classified as concentric, eccentric or plateau raised bog were delineated as
polygons. We used all massifs of these three types (mire-massif type "A" in the survey
database) and dissolved adjoining polygons into 564 contiguous raised-bog polygons with a
total area of 70 km^2^ (@fig-studyarea). TODO(JV): confirm that ridge raised bog (kanthøgmyr, A6) is
included in type A and should be, and whether atlantic raised bog is excluded by the
region definition alone.

Because the survey was designed to be complete within the areas it covered, the absence of
a mapped raised bog is informative there and nowhere else. We reconstructed the surveyed
area from the aerial-photo project coverages listed in the survey reports (13 orthophoto
projects flown 2008--2015, matched image strip by image strip to the reports) plus the
orthophoto-surveyed area given in @lyngstadKartleggingAvTypisk2016. The survey footprint
covers 110,065 km^2^ of southern, eastern and central Norway, and all Norwegian absences
were drawn from inside it (@fig-studyarea (B)). TODO(JV): check the footprint area and the count of
projects against the reports; the Hedmark 2012 survey has no strip table
(notebook 2025-11).

Norway was modelled on a 250 m grid in the European equal-area projection (EPSG:3035).
A cell was a raised-bog presence if its centre fell inside a raised-bog polygon (1,137
cells) and an absence candidate if its centre fell inside the survey footprint but not
inside a polygon (1.76 million cells).

### Europe: raised-bog records from the typical raised bog region

European raised-bog presences were taken from the Natura 2000 habitat inventory
[TODO(JV): citation for the Natura 2000 end-2021 spatial dataset], habitat types 7110
(active raised bogs) and 7120 (degraded raised bogs still capable of regeneration), within
the typical raised bog region of Europe (region IV of @tannebergerMiresEuropeRegional2021,
@fig-studyarea (A)). Natura 2000 sites are polygons that often contain a raised bog as one part of a
larger complex, so a site polygon cannot be used as a presence at 250 m resolution without
a rule for where in the polygon the bog is. We used two rules. Sites smaller than 1 km^2^
were used directly. Larger sites were used only where a vegetation-plot record of raised
bog vegetation (EUNIS habitat Q11 in the European Vegetation Archive plot database,
@chytryEUNISHabitatClassification2020) pinned the bog to a location inside the site; each
such plot became one presence point. Only sites with habitat data quality "good" were
used, and sites with representativity "D" (non-significant presence) were excluded.

This is deliberately narrow. Of the good-quality raised-bog sites in the region, 494
larger sites without a plot record (10,045 km^2^ of designated area) were not used as
presences. The loss costs statistical power but not climatic coverage: the median
warmest-quarter temperature of the discarded sites (15.7 °C) lies between that of the
small sites retained (15.4 °C) and the large sites with plots (16.0 °C), and the retained
small sites span the widest temperature range of the three sets (9.5--19.1 °C). The final
European presence set held 701 geometries (445 small site polygons and 256 plot points),
falling in 524 grid cells.

The European domain from which absences were drawn was region IV intersected with the
EU-27 (because Natura 2000 exists only in member states, so raised bogs elsewhere in the
region are unmapped rather than absent), with the country coverage of the European
Peatland Map (next section), and with the extent of our climate data, minus Norway. The
domain covers 495,223 km^2^ in ten countries (Finland, Sweden, Latvia, Lithuania,
Estonia, Poland, Austria, France, Germany and Czechia; @fig-studyarea (A)). It contains the whole
range of warmest-quarter temperature that Norway is projected to reach by 2071--2100 (see
Results), which is the property the European data were recruited for.

## A three-class response

### Why three classes

A raised bog is a climatic intermediate. Colder and wetter than the raised-bog band lie
other mire types (fens, aapa mires, blanket bogs); warmer and drier lie forest, heath and
farmland on mineral soil. A binary model of raised bog against everything else lumps these
two opposite flanks into one negative class, and the negatives that define the cold edge
of the niche have nothing in common with those that define the warm edge. Under warming
the relevant transition is away from the cold flank and towards the warm one, so a model
that cannot tell the flanks apart cannot say which way a bog is moving. We therefore
labelled every training cell as one of three classes: *raised bog*, *other peatland*, or
*non-peat*. The probability of raised bog is the quantity of interest; the split of the
remaining probability between the other two classes says what a site is predicted to
become. The same three labels were built on both the Norwegian and the European side, from
different sources but by the same logic (@tbl-frame).

### Norway: labels from the AR50 land-resource map

For Norwegian absence candidates we used the peatland class (class 60, myr) of the AR50
land-resource map [TODO(JV): NIBIO AR50 citation and version], rasterised at 50 m and
aggregated to the fraction of each 250 m cell mapped as peatland. Cells with a peatland
fraction of at least 0.5 were labelled *other peatland*; cells with a fraction below 0.1
were labelled *non-peat*; cells in between (mixed cells) and cells with no AR50 value were
excluded from training rather than assigned to either class. Of the 1.76 million absence
candidates, 1.32 million were non-peat, 61,850 other peatland, 177,860 mixed and 197,190
without a value. The peatland fraction was used only as a label and was not a predictor in
the model.

### Europe: labels from the European Peatland Map 2025

For European absence candidates we used the raster European Peatland Map 2025
[@tannebergerPeatlandMapEurope2017; TODO(JV): add Tegetmeyer et al. 2025 EPM2025 technical description to the library], a compilation of national peatland maps, resampled by majority to the
250 m grid within each country. Its map category 0 (no peatland) became *non-peat* and
category 1 (peat-dominated) became *other peatland*. Category 2 (peat in a soil mosaic)
was excluded, exactly as Norway's mixed cells were: the data producers already flag it as
the class where the extent of peat is uncertain. Inside a mapped country, no value means no
peatland; outside the mapped countries, no value means unknown, and those cells were
excluded rather than treated as non-peat. At 250 m the domain was 90.2% non-peat, 9.3%
peat-dominated and 0.5% soil mosaic.

Before absences were drawn, every cell that could be a raised bog was removed from the
European candidate pool with a deliberately generous exclusion mask: all Natura 2000
raised-bog and blanket-bog sites (7110, 7120, 7130) of any data quality, all raised-bog and
blanket-bog vegetation plots (EUNIS Q11 and Q12) buffered by one cell, and all polygons of
the vector European Peatland Map whose national peatland-type attribute contained "bog",
the whole union dilated by one cell. The mask removed 13.2% of the domain (69,289 km^2^).
Its generosity costs almost nothing in absence supply and ensures that a mapped raised
bog that did not qualify as a presence (for example a large site without a plot record)
became unlabelled rather than a false absence.

### One land-use and water screen for both blocks

Cells dominated by cropland, built-up land or open water carry no information about whether
climate can support peat, and their inclusion as non-peat would charge drainage,
cultivation and the sea to warming. We therefore screened every candidate cell of every
class on both blocks with one rule built from the 10 m ESA WorldCover map for 2021
[TODO(JV): WorldCover citation, Zanaga et al.]: a cell was dropped if more than 50% of
its area was cropland plus built-up land, or more than 50% was water plus unmapped (open
sea). The screen was applied before absences were drawn, so the draw was filled from
eligible cells. It kept 98.2% of Norwegian raised-bog cells (1,116 of 1,137), 89.9% of the
Norwegian absence pool, 95.2% of European raised-bog cells (499 of 524) and 79.5% of the
European absence pool. The two blocks fail the screen for different reasons, Norway mostly
on water and Europe mostly on human land cover, which is why the same rule had to be
applied to both: screening Norway alone would have manufactured a warm-flank asymmetry
instead of removing one.

### A climate-stratified absence draw

The two absence classes are far more numerous than raised bogs on both blocks, and the
non-peat pool in particular is dominated by climates far from any raised bog. Drawing
absences at random would fill the training set with cold uplands and leave the warm edge,
where the European data are needed, thin. We therefore drew a fixed budget of 25 absences
per raised-bog cell per absence class from each block (27,900 per class in Norway, 12,475
per class in Europe), spread as evenly as possible across 1 °C strata of mean
warmest-quarter temperature (bio10). Strata with fewer candidates than their share were
taken in full and the remainder redistributed. Strata warmer than the warmest Norwegian
training cell (17.1 °C) were guaranteed a minimum share before the general allocation, so
that the European block always contributed labelled cells beyond the Norwegian envelope.
The final pooled training frame held 82,359 cells (@tbl-frame).

## Predictors

Each cell carried 43 predictors (S1 Table). Thirty-two were climate variables from CHELSA
V2.1 [@kargerClimatologiesHighResolution2017; @kargerCHELSAV21Technical2021]: the 19
standard bioclimatic variables and 13 of the CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ variables that have future
projections [@brunGlobalClimaterelatedPredictors2022; @kargerBIOCLIMNovelSet2022] (growing
degree days and number of growing days above 0, 5 and 10 °C, growing-season length,
temperature and precipitation, frost-change frequency, snow-cover days, snow water
equivalent and potential net primary productivity). Current climate is the 1981--2010
climatology; future climate is the 2071--2100 climatology under SSP3-7.0 from the
GFDL-ESM4 model. TODO(JV): only one general circulation model and one scenario are used;
notebook 2026-09-12 raises adding a milder scenario. State the choice of GFDL-ESM4.

Two terrain variables, elevation and slope, were derived by aggregating a digital
elevation model to 250 m and then computing slope in degrees. For Norway the source was the
national 50 m terrain model [TODO(JV): Kartverket DTM50 citation]; for Europe, where that
model does not exist, elevation was fetched from AWS terrain tiles at about 90 m with the
elevatr package [TODO(JV): citation] and processed by the same aggregate-then-slope
recipe. Nine variables summarised deglaciation and long-term climate history from the
CHELSA-TraCE21k palaeoclimate series [TODO(JV): TraCE21k citation] sampled every 500 years
from 16 ka to the present: the time a cell has been continuously ice-free land, and the
mean and sum of annual temperature and precipitation over that ice-free period and over
the whole 16 ka. These express the time a site has had to accumulate peat and were the
same in both scenarios.

Climate and palaeoclimate layers were projected from their native 30 arc-second grid to
the 250 m grid for Norway and to a 5 km grid for Europe (no 250 m European stack was built;
both are resamples of the same source). Growing-degree, growing-season-temperature and
snow variables that CHELSA leaves undefined where the threshold is never crossed were set
to zero where all other layers had data. Growing-season precipitation is stored without
a no-data tag, so its no-data code was masked explicitly before resampling and then
treated the same way. TODO(gsp): the results below were produced before that step was
added and 8,987 training cells (all cold, bio10 <= 12.5 °C) carry the code; rerun the
pipeline and refresh every number marked TODO(gsp).

## Model-free description of the projection problem

Before fitting any model we asked two questions of the data alone. First, where does the
future climate of today's Norwegian raised bogs lie relative to the climates occupied
today by the three classes? Second, among the training cells that already have such a
climate, how common are raised bogs? The second question is an observational reading of
the same evidence the model will be asked to generalise, and it does not depend on a
learner.

For the first question we compared the 15 predictors that shift most under the scenario
between the three current classes and the 1,116 Norwegian raised-bog cells carried to their
2071--2100 climate. All 15 are temperature or degree-day measures; no precipitation
variable shifts by more than 0.4 standard deviations of its current spread. For the
second question we cross-tabulated the training cells on warmest-quarter temperature
(bio10; < 14, 14--16, 16--18 and > 18 °C) and growing-season precipitation (gsp; < 500,
500--650 and > 650 mm) and reported the observed prevalence of raised bog in each cell of
the grid alongside the share of future raised-bog cells that land there. Temperature is
the axis the projection travels; growing-season precipitation is the moisture axis with
the highest importance in the model and it barely changes under the scenario, so crossing
the two isolates the temperature effect. Raised bogs are ombrotrophic, so a warm-and-dry
analogue would say little about a warm-and-wet future, and the grid keeps the two apart.
The same grid was repeated with annual precipitation as the moisture axis.

## The model

We fitted one random forest to the pooled three-class frame with the randomForestSRC
package [TODO(JV): Ishwaran & Kogalur citation], using the package's balanced-sampling
recipe for imbalanced classes [@chenUsingRandomForest]: each of 1,000 trees was grown on a
class-balanced bootstrap sample (three times the size of the rarest class, drawn with
class-equalising weights), so that the 2% of cells that are raised bogs count as much as
either abundant class. The predicted class of a cell was the most probable of the three
(argmax), which for a balanced forest needs no separately tuned threshold. We used default
values for the number of variables tried at each split and the terminal node size; random
forests are insensitive to these at this sample size
[@valaviPredictivePerformancePresenceonly2022; @ludwigAssessingImprovingTransferability2023].
The data block (Norway or Europe) was carried through every table as bookkeeping and was
never a predictor: a forest allowed to split on it could learn "Europe" as a shortcut for
"warm" instead of learning the climate.

We note what the class probabilities are and are not. Because the forest was fitted under
a rebalanced prior, its probability of raised bog is not the probability that a cell is a
raised bog at the prevalence found in the landscape. It is a score that ranks cells and,
together with the two other scores, decides the predicted class. Everything below treats
it as such.

## Evaluating transfer into a warmer climate

### Partitions cut along summer temperature

A random cross-validation would test the model on cells with near-identical neighbours in
training and say nothing about the projection, which moves every Norwegian bog into a
climate warmer than any Norwegian training bog [@meyerPredictingUnknownSpace2021;
@linnenbrinkKNNDMCVKfold2024]. We therefore partitioned the training frame in
climate space along the axis the projection travels. The candidate axis was chosen among
predictors that change under the scenario by at least half a standard deviation of their
current spread (17 of the 32 climate predictors qualify) as the one with the highest
importance in the forest; that was warmest-quarter temperature (bio10). The 1,615
raised-bog cells were sorted on bio10 and cut into five equal groups of 323; the other
cells were assigned to the partition whose bog temperature range they fell in, with the
cuts between partitions placed midway between adjacent bog groups and the two end
partitions open-ended, so that every cell belongs to exactly one partition and cells warmer
than the warmest training bog are kept, in partition 5, rather than dropped (S2 Table;
TODO(JV): decide whether the partition table goes in the main text or supplement).

Two cross-validation arms were run on these partitions with the same learner. The
*pairwise* arm trained on one partition and tested on each of the other four (20 train--test
pairs); it is the harder extrapolation test but trains on a median of 5,042 cells against
the production model's 82,359, so its skill confounds extrapolation with data starvation.
The *leave-one-partition-out* arm trained on four partitions and tested on the fifth (5
folds, median 77,317 training cells); it is the arm that resembles the production model.
Reading the two together separates the cost of extrapolating from the cost of a small
training set. The leave-one-partition-out arm is quoted as the estimate of production
skill; the pairwise arm is the one the reliability curves are fitted on, for reasons given
in the next section.

Skill was summarised per fold as the 3 x 3 confusion matrix, per-class recall
(sensitivity), per-class one-vs-rest AUC, the macro AUC (mean over classes) and the macro
G-mean (geometric mean of the three recalls, which falls to zero if any class is
abandoned). All metrics were reported for the whole test partition and separately for the
Norwegian and European test cells, so that a good score on one block cannot mask a poor
score on the other. They were also reported separately for test cells warmer than the
warmest training bog and colder than the coldest, where the only meaningful quantity is
the rate at which the model wrongly calls such a cell a raised bog.

### Skill as a function of warming beyond the training bogs

A single cross-validated score describes the model on average, but the projection is read
at a specific place in climate space: about 3 °C warmer than the bogs the model learned
from. What matters is the model's skill *there*. Following the logic of pixel-wise
accuracy estimation [@meyerPredictingUnknownSpace2021;
@ludwigAssessingImprovingTransferability2023], we used the held-out predictions of the
pairwise arm as a calibration dataset and expressed each held-out cell's
position as its signed offset in warmest-quarter temperature from the median bio10 of the
raised bogs in that fold's training set. A cell at +2 °C was, for the model that scored it,
2 °C warmer than the typical raised bog it had seen. The signed offset was preferred to a
multivariate distance because the model treats warm-side and cold-side novelty
oppositely, and an unsigned distance pools the two.

The pairwise arm was used for this calibration, rather than the leave-one-partition-out
arm quoted for production skill, for two reasons. It reproduces the extrapolation the
projection makes: a model trained on one partition and tested on a distant one scores
held-out raised bogs far from the bogs it learned from, whereas a model trained on four
partitions has a close analogue for nearly every held-out bog and so places few raised-bog
cells at the offsets where the projection is read. Within the 10th--90th percentile band
of the mapped raised bogs' 2071--2100 offset (+1.7 to +3.8 °C), the pairwise arm holds
366 held-out raised-bog cells scored by four models; the leave-one-partition-out arm holds
32, scored by one. And it replicates: every bin of the axis is scored by four to six
independently fitted models, which is what a fold-level interval requires, whereas with
partitions cut on the same axis a leave-one-partition-out bin and a fold are nearly the
same object, and four of its eight bins are fed by a single model. The price is that the
curves describe models trained on a median of 5,042 cells, not the production model's
82,359, so the expected skill read from them is a floor on the production model's rather
than an estimate of it. The leave-one-partition-out point estimates are drawn alongside
for reference.

Held-out cells were binned into eight bins with equal numbers of raised-bog cells (about
800 each; every raised-bog cell is scored once by each of the four models that did not
train on it), so that the warm end of the axis, where the projection sits, is not resting
on a handful of presences, and skill was computed per bin. Because cells within a fold
share one model, uncertainty was estimated by resampling the 20 folds, not cells (cluster
bootstrap, 500 resamples). Every bin draws on four to six folds, so an interval is reported
for every bin; the intervals on the operating-point metrics are wide, and should be read
as such.

### Multivariate novelty and area of applicability

Warming along one axis is not the only way a projected cell can differ from the training
data. To capture novelty in all climate dimensions at once we computed the dissimilarity
index of @meyerPredictingUnknownSpace2021: the Euclidean distance from a cell to its
nearest training cell in standardised, importance-weighted predictor space, divided by the
mean distance between training cells. Three choices made this comparable everywhere it was
measured. The weights (median permutation importance over five fits of the production
learner to the whole training frame, 500 trees each) and the standardisation were frozen
once and reused for every fold and for the projection. The distance was computed over the 32 climate
predictors only: terrain and palaeoclimate are identical in both scenarios, cannot register
any projected change, and would only dilute the distance (they carry 58% of the
unrestricted importance mass, slope alone 43%). And the area of applicability threshold
was derived from held-out cross-validation distances (the Tukey upper fence of the
pairwise arm's held-out distances), as in the original method, rather than from
within-training distances, which with 82,000 densely packed cells measure training density
rather than attainable novelty. The dissimilarity index was used for the applicability
mask and as a second, retained axis for the skill curves; the map's expected skill was
read on the signed temperature offset.

## Projection and reliability mapping

The production forest, fitted on all 82,359 cells, was applied to every 250 m land cell of
mainland Norway under current and future climate, giving three class-probability layers
per scenario. Change at the mapped raised bogs was summarised per polygon as the mean of
each layer over the polygon's cells, the predicted class before and after, and the change
in the raised-bog score. For every projected cell we also computed its signed bio10 offset
from the production model's training bogs (median 15.53 °C), its dissimilarity index, and
the cross-validated recall and false-positive rate for raised bog interpolated from the
offset bins to the cell's offset; cells beyond the last bin inherit that bin's values,
and cells beyond the applicability threshold are flagged so that no estimate is read
there.

## Software

All analyses were run in R [TODO(JV): version] with the packages sf and terra for
spatial data [TODO(JV): citations], randomForestSRC for the forest, and the tidyverse for
data handling. The full pipeline is available at
<https://github.com/julienvollering/DMraisedbog>. TODO(JV): archive a release (Zenodo)
and cite it.

# Results

## Training data

The pooled training frame held 1,615 raised-bog cells, 1,116 Norwegian and 499 European,
against 25 absences per bog cell in each of the two other classes (@tbl-frame). The Norwegian
raised bogs occupy warmest-quarter temperatures of 12.1--16.5 °C (median 15.5 °C), and no
Norwegian training cell of any class is warmer than 17.1 °C. The European presences span
9.5--19.1 °C and so extend the warm edge of the raised-bog class by 2.6 °C, and the
European absences reach 21 °C. Of the 344,513 screened European absence candidates warmer
than any Norwegian training cell, the stratified draw placed 1,134 non-peat cells in each
1 °C stratum from 17 to 21 °C, against 745 per stratum in the cooler strata; other
peatland is scarce that warm (12,423 candidates above 17 °C, 518 above 18 °C) and all of
it up to the budget was taken.

## Where the future takes today's raised bogs, and what is observed there

Under SSP3-7.0 the mean warmest-quarter temperature at the 1,116 Norwegian raised-bog
cells rises from a median of 15.5 °C to 19.1 °C (range 14.8--20.2 °C), so that 48% of them
become warmer than the warmest raised bog in the pooled training data (19.1 °C, a European
one), and every one of the 15 most strongly
shifting predictors moves the bog cells past the current raised-bog distribution and into
the range of today's non-peat cells (@fig-occupancy (A); growing degree days above 5 °C, for example,
from a median of 1,354 to 2,096). Precipitation barely changes: growing-season
precipitation shifts by 0.36 standard deviations and annual precipitation by 0.22.

The climates the bogs are moving into are already sampled, by the European block. In the
wet column of the occupancy grid (growing-season precipitation above 650 mm), which holds
83% of the future raised-bog cells, the observed prevalence of raised bog is 8.5% at
14--16 °C, 4.1% at 16--18 °C and 0.19% at temperatures above 18 °C (7 raised bogs among
3,782 cells; @fig-occupancy (B), @tbl-occupancy). Ninety per cent of the future raised-bog cells fall in that
warmest band, three-quarters of them in its wet column: a 21-fold drop in observed
prevalence at constant moisture, on 3,782 sampled cells, with the moisture that raised bogs
need still present. The grid on annual precipitation shows the same pattern (0.34% raised
bog above 18 °C in the wettest column; S2 Table TODO).

Two caveats belong with this table. The warm evidence is entirely European and
geographically concentrated: the 4,081 training cells warmer than 18 °C lie in 16
one-degree squares between 45 and 49 °N (the Massif Central, Jura, Alpine foothills and
the Bohemian belt), with 60% of them in three squares, at elevations of 160--870 m. Matching
on temperature and precipitation does not match day length or evaporative demand, and the
effective sample size is far below the cell count. And the cold-wet cell of the grid
(< 14 °C, > 650 mm) is inflated by the 8,987 cells carrying the growing-season
precipitation no-data code (Methods; TODO(gsp): remove this sentence after the rerun);
its prevalence with those cells removed is about 0.9%. Neither caveat touches the warm
columns.

## Model fit and cross-validated skill

On its own out-of-bag cells the production forest recovered 89% of raised bogs (one-vs-rest
AUC 0.97), 85% of other peatland and 79% of non-peat, with a macro G-mean of 0.84. As
expected for a balanced forest, the raised-bog class was over-called: 7,484 cells were
predicted raised bog for 1,615 actual, a precision of 0.19.

Held-out skill was lower and depended strongly on how much the training set resembled the
production model (@tbl-cv). Leave-one-partition-out folds, with training sets of the
production model's size, reached a macro AUC of 0.79 and a macro G-mean of 0.48, recovering
78% of raised bogs; pairwise folds, trained on a fifth of the data, reached 0.73 and 0.37,
recovering 54%. Most of the difference between these arms is the cost of the small training
set rather than of extrapolating, so we quote the leave-one-partition-out arm as the
estimate of production skill under climate transfer.

Skill differed between the two data blocks in a specific way. Raised bogs were recovered
about equally well on both (78% in Norway, 77% in Europe), but Norwegian other peatland was
recovered at only 15% against 73% in Europe, with those Norwegian mires mostly called
non-peat, and European non-peat at 19% against 56% in Norway (@tbl-cv, S3 Table TODO
confusion by block). Slope is by far the most important predictor for the other peatland
contrast (S1 Table), and European mapped peatland is flatter than Norway's: 74% of
European other-peatland cells have a slope below 1° against 22% of Norwegian ones
(TODO(JV): verify; from notebook 2026-08-24), so the forest has learned a "peat is flat"
rule from the European block that it misapplies to Norwegian sloping mires. This weakness
lies on the flat-versus-steep axis, not on the climatic axis the study turns on.

Beyond the temperature range of the training bogs the model was asymmetric, and the
asymmetry is the most informative single result of the cross-validation. When the warmest
partition was held out (2,425 test cells warmer than every training bog, none of them a
raised bog), the model called *all* of them raised bog: a false-positive rate of 1.00
(pairwise arm 0.77). When the coldest partition was held out (17,961 cells colder than
every training bog) it called none of them raised bog. So the forest, asked about a
climate warmer than any raised bog it has seen, does not withdraw the raised-bog label; it
extends it. The projected loss reported below is therefore not an artefact of a model that
defaults to absence outside its training range. It is produced by the warm-flank labels
that are present in the production training set.

| Arm | Test cells | Folds | Median training cells | Macro AUC | Macro G-mean | Recall raised bog | Recall other peatland | Recall non-peat | FPR raised bog |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Leave-one-out | all | 5 | 77,317 | 0.79 | 0.48 | 0.78 | 0.49 | 0.43 | 0.43 |
| | Norway | 5 | 77,317 | 0.78 | 0.30 | 0.78 | 0.15 | 0.56 | 0.53 |
| | Europe | 5 | 77,317 | 0.76 | 0.28 | 0.77 | 0.73 | 0.19 | 0.33 |
| | warmer than all training bogs | 1 | 67,943 | 0.57 | -- | -- | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.00 |
| | colder than all training bogs | 1 | 23,430 | 0.76 | -- | -- | 0.10 | 0.99 | 0.00 |
| Pairwise | all | 20 | 5,042 | 0.73 | 0.37 | 0.54 | 0.41 | 0.55 | 0.32 |
| | Norway | 20 | 5,042 | 0.72 | 0.24 | 0.51 | 0.17 | 0.67 | 0.35 |
| | Europe | 20 | 5,042 | 0.72 | 0.31 | 0.57 | 0.56 | 0.36 | 0.28 |
| | warmer than all training bogs | 4 | 3,610 | 0.57 | -- | -- | 0.00 | 0.20 | 0.77 |
| | colder than all training bogs | 4 | 3,610 | 0.62 | -- | -- | 0.00 | 0.96 | 0.04 |

: **Cross-validated skill on partitions cut along warmest-quarter temperature,
by arm and by subset of the test cells** (means over folds). Recall is the share of cells
of a class predicted as that class; FPR is the share of cells not of the class predicted

## Skill against warming beyond the training bogs

Along the signed temperature offset, discrimination and the operating point behaved
differently (@fig-skill, @tbl-bins). The raised-bog AUC was 0.70--0.83 in the seven bins
up to +1.4 °C and fell to 0.64 (0.56--0.78) in the warm bin (+1.4 to +6.8 °C, median
+2.5 °C), which draws on the six folds whose test partition lay warmer than their training
partition. The operating point moved the other way. In the cold bin and within a degree of
the typical training bog the pairwise models recovered 43--53% of raised bogs at
false-positive rates of 0.10--0.16; from +0.4 °C upward recall rose through 0.47 and 0.74
to 0.81 (0.62--0.93) in the warm bin, and the false-positive rate through 0.22 and 0.28 to
0.48 (0.41--0.55). The leave-one-partition-out reference, whose models saw four
partitions, is sharper in the same direction: it recovered 12% of raised bogs in the cold
bin at a false-positive rate of 0.002, 89--99% between -0.7 and +0.6 °C, and 79% in its
warm bin at a false-positive rate of 0.55. On both arms, then, the forest asked about a
climate warmer than its training bogs extends the raised-bog label rather than withholding
it, consistent with the envelope result above; the production-sized model does so more
strongly, and withholds the label more strongly on the cold side, where it has learned
that bogs stop.

The 564 mapped raised bogs sit today at a median offset of -0.4 °C, in the bins where the
pairwise models recover about half of the raised bogs and the production-sized reference
over 90%. Under the 2071--2100 climate they sit at a median offset of +3.2 °C (90th
percentile +3.8 °C), inside the warm bin; 23% of the polygons (48% of their cells) lie
beyond the warmest raised bog in the production training set (+3.5 °C). The skill the map
can attach to them is the warm bin's: a recall of 0.81 (0.62--0.93) and a false-positive
rate of 0.48 (0.41--0.55), from six folds.

The same curves against the multivariate dissimilarity index are flat in discrimination
(raised-bog AUC 0.69--0.77 across a forty-fold range of novelty) while the false-positive
rate slides from 0.30 to 0.17 and recall varies between 0.41 and 0.66 without trend
(S1 Fig). That axis is dominated by cold and seasonally unusual cells rather than
warm ones, which is why it cannot carry the skill read for a warming projection; it is
retained for the applicability mask.

## Projected change at the mapped raised bogs

Under current climate the model reproduces the mapped distribution: the raised-bog score
averages 0.91 over the 564 polygons and 544 of them are predicted raised bog (@fig-projection (A, C);
@fig-lyngstad (A)). Under the 2071--2100 climate the score averages 0.16, it falls at 99% of the
polygons (median change -0.82; 5th and 95th percentiles -0.90 and -0.38), no polygon keeps
a score above 0.5, and 543 of the 544 predicted raised bogs are predicted non-peat, one
other peatland (@tbl-transitions; @fig-projection (B, D); @fig-lyngstad). The direction of the transition is the point
of the three-class response: the mapped raised bogs are not projected to become other
kinds of mire but to leave the peat-supporting climate altogether.

Over mainland Norway as a whole, the share of 2 km cells whose majority class is raised
bog falls from 3.3% to 0.2%, and other peatland from 22% to 10% (TODO(JV): these shares
are computed on 2 km aggregates for plotting; recompute at 250 m if they are to be quoted).
The few cells predicted raised bog in 2071--2100 lie in the far north-east and at scattered
inland sites (@fig-projection (D)). TODO(JV): whether to report "newly suitable" area at all; notebook
2026-06-05 frames the cold-flank transition (other peatland warming into the bog window)
as a second question.

| Predicted today | Predicted 2071--2100 | Polygons | Share |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Raised bog | Non-peat | 543 | 96.3% |
| Non-peat | Non-peat | 11 | 2.0% |
| Other peatland | Non-peat | 9 | 1.6% |
| Raised bog | Other peatland | 1 | 0.2% |

## Reliability of the projection where it is read

By the multivariate dissimilarity index the future projection domain is not extreme: its
median dissimilarity (0.28) is below the median of the held-out cross-validation cells
(0.55), its 90th percentile (0.63) is covered by the cross-validation's 90th percentile
(1.33), and no future cell exceeds the applicability threshold (1.97). At the mapped raised
bogs the future dissimilarity is 0.37, where the model still has many training neighbours.
That reading is optimistic in a specific way: the index measures distance to any training
cell, and the future climate of the bogs is close to European non-peat and other-peatland
cells, not to raised bogs. On the signed temperature axis the same cells sit beyond the
warmest training bog (@fig-reliability (A)). The two layers therefore say different things, and both are
part of the answer: the projection is well supported by labelled data of the two other
classes, and it is an extrapolation with respect to raised bogs specifically. The expected
skill layer (@fig-reliability (C)) carries the warm bin's recall of 0.81 over most of southern Norway
and the interior bins' recall of about 0.43--0.53 over the mountains and the north, so
that the median expected recall over the domain is 0.43. At the mapped raised bogs the
expected recall is 0.81 (0.62--0.93) under the future climate against 0.46 (0.16--0.78)
today, and the expected false-positive rate 0.48 against 0.13: the operating point the
projection is read at favours calling raised bog, which makes the non-peat verdict at
these polygons stronger evidence than the same verdict from a neutral operating point
would be.

![**Reliability layers over the 2071--2100 projection domain.** (A) Warmest-quarter
temperature offset from the production model's training raised bogs. (B) Dissimilarity
index on the frozen ruler (applicability threshold 1.97; no cell exceeds it). (C)
Expected recall of raised bog, read from the offset bins of @fig-skill. Rasters aggregated to
2 km.](figures/fig_reliability.png){#fig-reliability}

# Discussion

TODO(JV): not drafted. Points the Results are written to support: (i) the model-free
occupancy table carries the conclusion and the model adds the map; (ii) the envelope
result (the forest extends the raised-bog label into warmer climates when the warm labels
are withheld) is the reply to "the model just defaults to absence outside its range";
(iii) formation versus persistence: occurrence-based evidence says which climates
maintain raised bogs today, existing bogs are landforms with self-maintaining hydrology,
so the projection is a loss of climatic suitability as currently expressed, not a
disappearance date (notebook 2026-08-21; @joostenMiresPeatlandsEurope2017 p. 135); (iv)
the warm evidence is European, southern and geographically clustered; (v) one scenario and
one climate model; (vi) the other-peatland weakness in Norway is a terrain-source
confound, not a climatic one.
